name: Scleral whitening / conjunctivectomy

card.summary: Elective surgery that removes or cauterises conjunctival tissue to make the whites of the eyes look whiter; published reports are limited to case reports of late complications.
card.note: Case reports describe regrowth of redness and severe scleral necrosis years after the procedure.

quick.overview:
Scleral whitening, also called cosmetic eye whitening or conjunctivectomy, is an elective operation aimed at making the visible white of the eye look whiter by removing or treating the surface tissue that carries blood vessels. One branded version is called I-BRITE.

The literature on the cosmetic procedure is thin. The published material found consists mainly of individual case reports describing late problems and a case where a patient used painted contact lenses to mask returning redness.
quick.mechanism: As described in the case literature, the procedure involves dissecting the conjunctiva and Tenon's capsule, applying cautery and using mitomycin C, an agent that limits tissue regrowth. The goal is to prevent visible blood vessels and redness from returning.
quick.risks: A case report describes severe pain, scleral inflammation and necrosis in both eyes nine years after the procedure, treated with immunosuppressive therapy. Another report describes recurrent conjunctival redness five years afterward. No controlled trials of the cosmetic procedure were found.

lead: Scleral whitening, also called cosmetic eye whitening or cosmetic conjunctivectomy, is an elective procedure intended to make the white of the eye appear whiter by removing or treating the conjunctival tissue and its blood vessels. One commercially named version is I-BRITE [1].

According to published case descriptions, the operation involves dissection of the conjunctiva and Tenon's capsule, cautery and application of mitomycin C [1]. Mitomycin C is an antiproliferative drug used in several eye surgeries.

No controlled studies of the cosmetic procedure were identified. The published literature consists of case reports describing late complications, including surgically induced scleral necrosis, and the recurrence of conjunctival redness [1][2].

paras: Case reports describe the procedure as conjunctival and Tenon's capsule dissection with cautery and mitomycin C application, performed for cosmetic reasons in people who dislike visible redness or blood vessels on the white of the eye [1]. The term conjunctivectomy refers to surgical removal of conjunctival tissue.

A 2023 case report described a 36-year-old woman who developed severe pain, scleral inflammation and necrosis in both eyes nine years after an I-BRITE procedure. An extensive workup was negative for other causes, and she improved with aggressive immunosuppressive therapy [1].

A 2020 case report described a 37-year-old man with recurrent conjunctival redness five years after eye-whitening conjunctivectomy with mitomycin C. He was counselled against repeat surgery and fitted with white-painted scleral contact lenses to mask regrown vessels, with a reported good cosmetic result and comfort [2].

No studies found. Published evidence for the cosmetic procedure is limited to individual case reports [1][2]. Studies of conjunctival surgery for pterygium, a medical condition, are a separate body of research.
